div.p: Ravenscar-Java is a subset of Java (augmented by the Real-Time Specification for Java) targeted at high-integrity real-time systems. It has recently been extended to support multiple applications of mixed criticality on the same Java platform. A two level scheduling model is used to achieve temporal isolation between applications. This paper presents the general schedulability analysis for the approach, describes how the approach can be implemented using standard real-time POSIX facilities, illustrates how the analysis can be modified to take into account the implementation, and uses the prototype implementation to evaluate the accuracy of the analysis models.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Over the last decade there has been a trend for large realtime distributed systems to move from federated architectures (where each application has its own dedicated computing resources) towards integrated architectures (where applications share the same computing resources). More recently, there has been a desire to move to Java-based realtime systems; this has resulted in the development of the Real-time Specification for Java (RTSJ) [6] [22]. For highintegrity systems, Ravenscar-Java [17] has been proposed as a suitable subset of Java and the Real-Time Specification for Java (RTSJ).

Where applications are executed within the context of a virtual machine, running multiple computations (called "isolates" [21] in the Java world) in a single instance of a safe language virtual machine can improve performance and overall platform scalability, and realize the full potential of language-provided safety and protection [10]. The goal of the Ravenscar-Java Isolates work is to investigate the feasibility of supporting multiple real-time applications (of different integrity levels) within the Ravenscar real-time virtual machine [8] [9], without having to engineering every-thing to the highest integrity level. One requirement of this computation model is that temporal isolation between different applications must be achieved. Temporal isolation (temporal firewalls) is the name given to the partitioning of resources (in the time domain) between subsystems within a larger system. Each subsystem is given a temporal service contract, so that its temporal behaviour can be validated independently of the other subsystems [16]. This property ensures that the temporal behavior of each subsystem does not depend on the behavior of any other subsystems.

This paper briefly reviews the Ravenscar-Java Isolates approach for achieving temporal isolation for different integrity level applications in section 2. Section 3 then presents the schedulability analyses for Ravenscar-Java Isolates. The overheads of an implementation are also considered in this section. Section 4 describes the prototype implementation that has been created to experiment with and to evaluate the approach. Initial results are discussed. Section 5, briefly considers related work, and the conclusions from this study are given in section 6.

div.head: The Scheduling Regime between Ravenscar-Java Isolates
div.p: Temporal isolation is usually achieved by scheduling and resource reservation techniques. The RTSJ supports priority-based scheduling, so this is the preferred scheduling regime within an isolate. Essentially, there are four approaches that could be taken when scheduling between isolates. The first approach is the single-level priority based scheduling with CPU budgets enforced. Here, the scheduler schedules all the threads of all isolates according to a global priority. This approach has the advantage that the scheduling of threads1 is responsive, but it requires global analysis for all isolates.

The second is the APEX approach [1][2]; here, time slicing between isolates is performed according to a static schedule, with fixed priority scheduling within isolates. Each isolate is guaranteed an amount of time within a period, so global analysis is straight forward. The main disadvantage is that a high priority thread that becomes runnable outside its isolate time slice must wait for the next time slice. The scheduling of threads in the isolate is not responsive, and large release jitter can occur. The third approach treats each isolate as an RTSJ's processing group [6] [7] and uses global fixed priority scheduling. This approach groups a set of scheduling objects together with the CPU capacity that is recharged periodically. The thread of the isolate is eligible for execution as long as its processing group has some CPU budget left. The threads are more responsive especially for sporadic threads, however more complex scheduling analysis is needed for the system (and indeed, in general, the approach is intractable [7]).

The fourth approach combines the good features of APEX and processing group parameters, and this is the one adopted by our extended Ravenscar-Java Virtual Machine (RJVM). The scheduling between isolates is priority based scheduling and the CPU consumptions are bound by using processing group parameters with CPU budgets recharged periodically. In effect, each isolate is serviced by a deferrable server [18] but the server schedules each thread within the isolate according to their individual priorities. Large release jitter can be avoided for the threads of higher priority isolates. Schedulable objects of a high priority isolate can be scheduled for execution when released as long as the isolate has CPU budget left. Ravenscar-Java targets hard real-time systems. All the threads must meet their deadline. The priority assignment for isolates is deadline monotonic priority assignment scheme based on the shortest deadline thread of each isolates. However, other more optimal priority assignment models can also be used [11]. To minimize the release jitter of threads within isolates, the period of an isolate is constrained to the greater common divisor of all the periodic real-time threads of the isolate.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: To calculate the worse case response time of threads, a two level scheduling analysis approach is adopted. First, the worst case response time of each server is calculated; that is the time required to guarantee that the isolate server obtains its capacity, then we calculate the response times of threads within their servers. Of course, if an isolate cannot get its budget within its period, then an alternative allocation is required.

div.head: The First Scheduling Level Implementation
div.p: Few, if any, real-time operating systems currently allow flexible servers with execution-time budgets. However, many allow a single thread within a process to have a budget. Given the requirement to execute multiple applications in the same virtual machine, each isolate is mapped to a schedulable thread in the underlying RTOS; consequently, the scheduling within isolates is based on the green thread model -in that the scheduling within isolates is transparent to the underlying RTOS. There are three approaches to implementing the first level scheduling. The first approach is to implement a periodic budget server provided by the underlying RTOS and each isolate is mapped down to a periodic budget server. This approach needs to modify the kernel of the supporting RTOS. The second approach is to use the facilities of some RTOS in which applications can define their own schedulers such as SHARK [13] and MaRTE OS [19]. However, these two solutions need a particular RTOS and the portability of Ravenscar-JVMs is compromised.

The third approach is to only use the facilities of Real-Time POSIX [15] to implement the two level scheduling model. Each isolate is mapped to a Real-Time POSIX thread with the isolates original priority and a background priority, and a monitor Real-Time POSIX thread, which manages all isolates. Each isolate thread is armed with a real-time periodic timer for the budget recharging time, a one shot budget overrun timer based on the CPU clock of the thread and a one shot timer for the timer queue of threads within isolates. The isolate monitor thread acts as a real-time signal interpreter. It runs at the highest priority in the system, and waits for signals from isolate threads, handles the signals and wait for further signals. When an isolate finishes its budget, it sends a budget overrun realtime signal. The monitor catches the signals and set the pri-ority of the isolates to its background priority. The budget recharge timer periodically sends a budget recharge signal. The monitor catches the signal and reset the isolate to its original priority, and reset the budget timer. When a RTSJ thread is to be woken, another real-time signal is generated. The monitor catches the signal and handles it. When an asynchronous I/O operation is finishing, a real-time signal is also generated and the monitor notifies the related isolates to handle it.

div.head: The Second Scheduling Level Implementation
div.p: In the second-level scheduling, each isolate has its own runtime data structures for scheduling. Each isolate has runnable queues for each priority, a timer queue for threads sleeping and an asynchronous I/O queue for threads waiting asynchronous I/O operations. When an isolate is scheduled, the first thread of the available highest priority runnable queue is scheduled to execute. The scheduling of threads with the same priorities is first-in-first-out scheduling. When Java threads wait for a timing event, they are put into the isolate timer queue sorted by their wake-up times. The isolate' wakeup timer is set to the earliest wake-up time of the sleeping threads. When the isolate monitor receives a thread wakeup signal, the threads due to run are moved from the timer queue to the appropriate runnable queues. This operation can either be performed immediately by the isolate monitor after receiving thread wake up signals or be performed by the isolates after been told by the monitor that some threads are waking and need to be moved into runnable queues. If it is performed by the monitor, the execution of all other isolates will be affected. The temporal isolation of applications is compromised. Our solution is that when thread are waking, the monitor tells the related isolate to search the timer queue. If there are higher priority threads waking, the new waking highest priority thread will be switched in for execution.

div.head: Experimental Evaluations
div.p: A prototype implementation is carried out on the MaRTE OS 1.56 bare machine version [19]. A system which contains three isolates each with six periodic threads is used to evaluate our approach under different utilizations. The timing properties of isolates and their threads are listed: The timing scale in the table is microseconds. The higher priority threads run before the low priority threads. The worse case execution time (WCET) of each thread is measured on the prototype implementation. The runtime overhead of the first level scheduling is measured by executing the measuring isolates with different number of isolates. First, the single isolate is executed and the worse case response time is measured. Then, the isolate is executed with the other two isolates and the worse case response time is taken again. The difference of the response time is taken as the first levelscheduling overhead. The runtime overhead of the second level scheduling is measured by executing threads with different number of threads within the same isolate. The smallest safe bound of WCET is chosen based on the accuracy of the testing platform which is 1 millisecond. Three versions of the prototype implementations are used to evaluate our approach. The first background enable version (denoted by BE) allows lower priority isolates to run earlier and can use up any gain time by executing at a background priority. The second no background version (denoted by NBE) does not allow any isolates use up any gain time after it uses up all its capacity. It can run only when it has capacity left. The third no slack version (denoted by NS) lets all isolates use up their capacity and no slack computation is given to lower priority isolates, but the isolate can use the gain time by executing at a background priority.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: JSR121 [21] first proposed the notion of an isolate and provided programming-level support for managing and communicating with separate Java programs. However, JSR121 does not address resource isolation issues such as CPU, memory usage etc. A subset of JSR121 is defined for J2ME, however, it still has a complex computational model and the rendezvous communication model between isolates does not address the issue of temporal isolation. RTSJ [6] provide facilities to bound the CPU usage of threads, however, all these facilities are restricted to threads within a single Java application.

Dillenberger et al [12] introduces an approach where execution of a new Java application involves creation and initialization of a new instance of the Java virtual machine; but they share a memory region to stored data that can be re-used by all the instances of JVM. Loading, linking and verifying classes happens only once. This provides total application isolation and reduced startup time of application. However, the overall platform scalability is compromised and it might suffer high cost of the first level scheduling.

KaffeOS [3] provides a solution to target the problem of running untrusted applications and prevent denial-ofservice attacks. It supports the operating system abstraction of processes to control their resource consumption. If the resource demands are too high, the Java applications will be terminated. To account for the memory consumption and GC time, each application has its own heap which is separately garbage collected. Shared heaps need to be created for directly sharing objects between processes. A kernel heap is used for new created objects of trusted code. From a real-time perspective, this hierarchy memory management is highly inefficient and unpredictable. The direct objects sharing and kernel heap sharing break the spatial and temporal isolation of application.

The J-Kernel [14] and Balfanz and Gong [4] achieve multi-application support based on class loader protection without making changes to the JVM. The spatial and temporal behaviour of applications are tightly coupled. This approach replicates application code and may result undesirable inter-application interactions.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Using priorities and CPU budgets for each application captures the different timing requirements for different applications, and also protects the computation resources of each application in the same platform. The application scheduling entities (isolates) and the scheduling entities within applications (threads) are mapped to the scheduling entities of the RTOS and the Ravenscar-JVM. The two level analysis model matches the two level implementation model.

The prototype implementation shows that for high utilizations, the pessimism between the predicted response time and the measured response time is 1.16 on average. For low utilization, the response times of lower priority isolates is significant improved as they are allowed to run earlier and can use up any gain time by executing at a background priority.
